newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Gecamines moves hard currency accounts.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Gecamines moves hard currency accounts.

text.p: Zaire's Gecamines, which closed its head offices in Lubumbashi earlier this week fearing civil war would engulf the city, will resume normal business on Monday, a senior manager told Reuters on Friday.

"We'll start up again on Monday without fail. As you can see there is not a single broken window," said Jean Nawej Yav, administration and payroll director of the state-owned copper and cobalt producer.

Other company sources said Gecamines had already arranged to transfer its hard currency accounts from Kinshasa to Lubumbashi so dollar payments for its mineral exports would no longer fall into the hands of those around President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"We've already changed all our accounts. So the money will now come straight to Lubumbashi," one source said. "In the past, the dollars used to stay in Kinshasa while we were reimbursed in Zaire notes printed locally."
The sources said company revenue was about $8.0 million a month and estimated that the company was working at around 10 percent capacity. There was no way to confirm the figures.

News of the closure of the company's offices in Lubumbashi on Monday in the face of advancing rebel troops underpinned a rise in the cobalt price to around $25 a pound in London this week. Zairean cobalt production of some 5,000 tonnes a year accounts for roughly one fifth of global supply.
"We have just had the Kolwezi operation on the radio asking for their salaries and we are getting those ready for them right now," Nawej Yav said.
The rebel forces of Laurent Kabila captured Lubumbashi, Zaire's second-largest city, on Wednesday with ease.

By Friday shops were reopening, streets were crowded and there were long lines at petrol stations that had been closed during days of high tension as the rebel army advanced and the government reinforced its troops.

Officials said reports of widespread looting by inhabitants after the rebels took the city were grossly exaggerated. They said four or five shops in the centre of town had been looted, but rebel units moved quickly to stamp out the pillaging and seven people were shot dead.

Deputy governor of Shaba province Donatien Mwitaba said he was confident the copper and cobalt mining company could quickly be relaunched and modernised with help from foreign partners attracted by the prospect of an end to Mobutu's dictatorial rule.

Mwitaba said international business clearly saw rebel leader Laurent Kabila as someone they could work with. "With Kabila's growing international credibility we think it will be possible to relaunch Gecamines very rapidly," he said in an interview.

"There are a certain number of privatisation and joint venture possibilities. There were offers already circulating, but I think now we can enlarge on these. Before, the potential partners were a bit reticent as they were doing business with a decadent regime."

Mwitaba said potential partners could come from South Africa or the United States: "These are the countries which have the financial capacity to help us develop and now we will have the political stability that these partners seek. There will be a rebirth of confidence."
Mwitaba said Sizarail, a Belgian-South African consortium that runs the railway in the area, had also reopened. The company could not be reached to confirm this.
Sizarail is responsible for transporting copper and cobalt from mines in Zaire's mineral-rich Shaba province, most of which Kabila's rebels have captured in their advance from the eastern border.
